content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85. I used 42 of the 60 budget points.

**What decided it:**
1. I trained L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3, so each of those rules had been seen once. The target task L4-S4-M4 had all-new rules, and its mapping matched the trained tasks on at most 0.1875 of inputs. It needed **54 and 53** examples to reach criterion.
2. I then trained L1-S4-M4 and L4-S3-M2. Together they contain the target's three rules once each, but their mappings share **0%** of responses with the target, so its highest similarity to any trained task stayed at 0.1875.
3. The target then needed 9, 37, 34, 24, 16 and 22 examples, a **mean of about 24**, roughly half the earlier cost.

A holistic learner would show no drop, because the target was no more similar to anything trained. A factor-when-justified learner would also show no drop: with k = 2 or 3, L4, S4 and M4 had each appeared only once, so none could be reusable parts yet. Only a part-based learner predicts the drop.

An earlier test pointed the same way but more weakly. L2-S1-M3 (no new rules) averaged about 20 examples and L4-S4-M3 (two new rules) about 30, even though both matched the trained tasks equally (0.375). With noise of about ±12 per test, that gap alone wasn't conclusive.

**Why not higher confidence:** the tests are very noisy (one task gave 1 and 36 on back-to-back runs). The decisive "before" number also rests on only two samples, which I took before I had planned this design, and training can't be undone to retest.
